issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: For a trauma type of witnessed other trauma, the appraisal that others can see what happened to me by looking at me is hard to reconcile unless there was also direct victimization or visible injury. The rest of the profile centers on witnessing, guilt about failing to protect, and anger that perpetrators were not held accountable, which fits. This item implies a conspicuous personal mark or shame signal not otherwise supported by the triggers, memory, or strategies, so it is clinically incoherent within this profile.

vignette:
María had spent most of her life in fabric rooms, fitting rooms, and show spaces, shaping dresses for other people’s milestones. But at 70, she spoke of one winter afternoon in the language of a scene that had never stopped unfolding. Years earlier, while visiting relatives in another city, she had witnessed a violent accident outside a market: a car skidded on wet pavement, struck an older man, and left him crumpled in the street while bystanders froze. María had been close enough to hear the impact and the stunned silence afterward, close enough to see the color drain from his face and to feel the cold air on her skin as she stood unable to move. What lodged in her mind was not only what she saw, but her certainty that she should have done more. She had the sense that if she had stepped in faster, shouted louder, or somehow taken control of the moment, she might have protected him. Instead, she remembers herself as passive and ashamed, and she has come to believe that the people who caused it faced no consequences while the wrong person carried the guilt.

In the weeks and years that followed, the memory would force its way into her mind when she did not want it, arriving with such force that it felt less like remembering than being pulled back inside the street. When it came, it was not a picture alone but a full bodily return: the smell of exhaust, the slick shine of the pavement, the sting of cold air on her hands, the sound of tires and frightened voices all at once. Because the memory came back with such force, María began to notice related things everywhere; a winter draft, a wet sidewalk, or the sharp sound of brakes could seize her attention before she had time to think, and those ordinary moments would immediately start to feel like warnings. She found herself bracing for the scene to return whenever the weather turned cold or she stepped near traffic, as if the memory had taught her to scan for its echoes in advance. Even now, an unexpected sensation against her skin can unlock it without warning. A draft from an open doorway, a burst of winter air in the grocery aisle, the chill of a metal chair at work can suddenly carry her back into that exact moment, and she becomes rigid before she can make sense of why.

Those intrusions have shaped how María lives at home and at work. She has started avoiding anything that reminds her of loss, including family photographs after funerals and conversations that turn toward people who have died. When a trigger catches her off guard, María cuts herself off from it as quickly as she can — she will leave a room, change the subject, or skip the conversation entirely because staying with it makes her feel as if the scene is opening again in front of her. She no longer watches the evening news, especially reports of crashes, street violence, or disasters, because one image is enough to set off the whole thing. At her design studio, where clients expect her to stay engaged and collaborative, she finds herself pushing away even positive feelings if they begin to soften her guard. When a fitting goes well or a granddaughter calls with good news, she feels a brief lift and then immediately mistrusts it, as though joy leaves her exposed. That sense of exposure has made her more cautious, more withdrawn, and more likely to pull away from anything that might remind her of what was lost.

The more she has tried to avoid those reminders, the more her world has narrowed to places and routines she thinks she can control. Yet control itself has become one of her sharpest triggers. And once that helplessness had taken hold, it made the memory surge back even faster, so that a small disruption or a moment of feeling cornered could drop her straight back into the market scene. The thought that she had failed to protect the man in the street then made every reminder feel more dangerous, and the more vividly she remembered, the more she watched for the next cue that might bring it all rushing in again. If a train of thought or a small disruption makes her feel cornered, her body reacts as if danger is already present. She watches doorways, checks the streets before crossing, and grows tense around any situation where she cannot decide what happens next. This vigilance is not comforting for long; it keeps the accident alive in the background of ordinary days. A news headline glimpsed on someone else’s phone, a colleague mentioning a recent hit-and-run, or the cold touch of a fitting room mirror against her forearm can summon the memory before she has time to brace herself, and once it arrives, she is flooded with the same conviction that she failed to protect the man in the street.

When the memory breaks through, it seems to confirm everything she fears about herself. She returns to the thought that she should have intervened, and from there the guilt hardens into a broader judgment: the event happened because of the way she acted, or failed to act, and the people responsible simply walked away. That appraisal intensifies the pull of the memory, and the memory in turn sharpens her sense of blame, making the scene feel present and morally unfinished. In that state, even neutral sensations become charged. A sudden drop in temperature, a news report on the radio in the studio, or the loss of control she feels when a memory appears without warning can all make her more alert for another return, as if she is waiting for the next blow.

By the time María came to treatment, she was exhausted by the narrowing of her life. Her work, once a source of pride and connection, had become something she moved through carefully, trying to avoid cold rooms, distressing news, and any conversation about death or grief. She wanted help because she was tired of feeling trapped by the same afternoon, tired of flinching at the weather and the television, and frightened that if she kept shutting out the good parts of life she would disappear into fear and guilt. What she hopes for now is not to forget what happened, but to be able to remember it without being taken back into it, and to believe that she can still live with her husband, her family, and her work without the accident ruling every room she enters.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette describes triggers and avoidance/safety behaviors, but it does not clearly state that the triggers themselves cause the maladaptive strategies within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."

  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."

  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."

  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
